hook_clip: My spec let one standup update ping everyone in the Slack channel.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of Geekbot a remote team needs. Everyone gets the same questions at nine thirty in their own time zone, and answers in writing. Blockers stay open until someone resolves them. And a daily summary goes out by email and to Slack.

The core rule is fair counting. An update is on time before the due time, late after it, and missed if the day ends without one. Days someone is out of office are never counted as missed. And nobody answers a check-in for someone else, not even a manager.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation. Check-ins, reports and blockers. The scheduled job, out of office and notifications. Then insights, export and pause. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser.

Here's what it built. The Product daily feed shows three of six reported, with Priya's and Maya's updates. Jo's late check-in shows what she said last time, and her open blocker. The schedule preview asks everyone at nine thirty in their own zone, so Priya's prompt goes out at four in the morning UTC. The outbox logged a reminder, a prompt, a nudge to Jo and the daily summary. Insights counts Tom four of five, with his two away days left out. And on a phone, Jo fills in the same form.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all thirty-two checks passed, along with one hundred and sixty-seven automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The test build exposed seventy-three places where Claude had to guess. Text people typed went to Slack as it was, so one update could ping the whole channel. Nothing said whether out of office, saved after the day closed, turns a missed update into away. And the built-in time zone list only knew Kolkata by its old name. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't production-ready. Production sign-in, real email delivery, a working Slack channel, a hosted scheduler and hosting were never tested. Check those yourself before your team relies on it.

So is it worth building? Geekbot's Starter plan is free for up to ten users, with three months of history. Basic costs two dollars fifty per participant a month, billed yearly, so twenty-five people pay seven hundred and fifty dollars a year. Build it if your team spans time zones and you want fair participation numbers and blockers you can track. Buy it if your team wants to answer inside Slack or Teams, or needs anonymous check-ins and AI summaries.
cues: free for up to ten users

scenes.text: Everything is in one file. The data model, eighteen rules, the seed data, four phase prompts and thirty-two checks, with all seventy-three fixes included.
